slides.text: Johar Gandhi is The Reminiscence Book of Record of the Freedom Fighters of the Diversity Land of Erstwhile Central Province of British India, and the two visits of Mahatma Gandhi in Chhattisgarh.
slides.visualDescription: Title card: Ancient Chhattisgarh forts silhouetted at dawn over dense Sal forest. Gold text reads MOHANDAS — The Land of 36 Forts. Ink-wash illustration, ochre and deep green palette, cinematic widescreen.

slides.text: Before Gandhi, before the British, before the Mughals — this land had a name. Dakshin Kosal. The southern kingdom. Mentioned in the Ramayana, revered in the Mahabharata, contested by the mightiest empires on the subcontinent. Chhattisgarh is not a young land. It is one of the oldest continuously inhabited regions of India — a land of 135,192 square kilometres, draped in dense Sal forests, veined by six major rivers, and anchored by mountains that have never bent to any conqueror. The Mahanadi does not merely flow here — it is born here, rising from the Sihawa hills before carving its way to the Bay of Bengal. Three thousand years of history are buried in this soil. The question is not who came here. The question is: who was here first?
slides.visualDescription: Aerial ink-wash illustration of ancient Dakshin Kosal — dense Sal forests, rivers glinting silver, ancient settlements visible through the canopy. The Mahanadi originates in golden light at the Sihawa hills. A cartographic style map dissolves into a living landscape. Deep greens, ochre, and midnight blue.

slides.text: Thirty-six forts. That is what the name means. Chhattis — thirty-six. Garh — fort. Scattered across hills and river bends and forested plateaus, each fort was once a kingdom, a court, a civilization. The Nala dynasty ruled here in the 5th century. The Sharabhapuriyas shaped the Mahanadi basin. The Somavamshis built temple complexes that rivaled the grandest architecture of medieval India. And then came the Kalachuris of Tripuri — whose 400-year reign transformed Chhattisgarh into a centre of political power, cultural refinement, and religious scholarship. By the time the Marathas arrived in 1741 under the Bhonsle clan of Nagpur, they inherited not a wilderness — but a civilisation already thousands of years in the making. Thirty-six forts. Thirty-six stories. Not one of them adequately told.
slides.visualDescription: A dramatic panoramic silhouette at dusk — 36 ancient forts rising against an amber sky on hills and riverbanks across a vast landscape. Each fort glows with a dim interior light. Timeline text appears briefly at the bottom: Nala dynasty 5th c. → Kalachuris 10th–13th c. → Marathas 1741. Ink-wash illustration, cinematic widescreen.

slides.text: Walk into the ruins of Sirpur on the banks of the Mahanadi and you walk into the 7th century. The Lakshmana Temple here — built entirely in brick — is one of the finest specimens of Gupta-period architecture in all of India. Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Hiuen Tsang passed through this region and recorded its prosperity with astonishment. Nearby, Bhoramdeo rises from the Maikal hills — an 11th-century Shiva temple so breathtaking in its sculptural detail that it has been called the 'Khajuraho of Chhattisgarh.' Then there is Ratanpur — the ancient Kalachuri capital — and Malhar, where coins and ruins from the 1st century BCE still surface from the earth after rains. Chhattisgarh is an open archive. Its soil remembers everything. The tragedy is that for centuries, the world chose not to listen.
slides.visualDescription: Close-up of the intricately carved pillars of Sirpur's Lakshmana Temple — red brick glowing in morning light. Cut to the soaring spire of Bhoramdeo Temple against misty Maikal hills. Then ancient Ratanpur fort ramparts, and a farmer's hand holding a corroded ancient coin unearthed from Malhar's soil. Reverent, cinematic. Sepia and ochre tones.

slides.text: Nearly half of Chhattisgarh is forest. The Sal, the Teak, the Tendu — they cover the land like a green mantle pulled tight over ancient bones. Thirty-two percent of the population belongs to tribal communities — the Gond, the Baiga, the Halba, the Kamar, the Oraon — peoples with their own languages, cosmologies, legal traditions, and relationships with the earth that predate every empire that claimed to rule them. The Bastar plateau, the Hasdeo coalfields, the Maikal range — these are not merely geographical features. They are living kingdoms of a culture that British cartographers drew lines around but could never contain. When the British arrived and began extracting timber, taxing forests, and redirecting rivers for their canals — they did not encounter a passive people. They encountered a civilization that had survived for millennia by understanding exactly what it meant to defend its land.
slides.visualDescription: Sweeping aerial view of Chhattisgarh's dense forest canopy — unbroken green stretching to every horizon, rivers cutting silver paths through the green. Then ground level: tribal community life — Gond dancers, Baiga elders, forest paths, village fires. A British surveyor's map being drawn over this living reality. The contrast between the map and the land. Cinematic, green and gold palette.

slides.text: The British came. And they brought something Chhattisgarh had never truly faced: systematic, bureaucratic extraction. The Central Provinces were formed in 1861. Chhattisgarh — with its forests, its coal, its iron ore, its agricultural river basins — was the crown jewel of that formation. Canal taxes were levied on farmers who had irrigated their own land for generations. Forest rights were extinguished by legislation. Tribal communities were criminalised for practising traditions older than the British Parliament itself. By the dawn of the 20th century, Chhattisgarh was a land of deep, organised grievance — politically awakening under leaders like Madhavrao Sapre, Sundarlal Sharma, and Vamanrao Lakhe, who had begun building the intellectual and social foundations of resistance long before Gandhi ever set foot in the region.
slides.visualDescription: British tax collectors at a village in Chhattisgarh — a ledger, a uniformed officer, farmers standing with strained, dignified faces. Then: a lamp-lit room where Madhavrao Sapre edits his Hindi newspaper Chhattisgarh Mitra — the first Hindi journal in the region, 1900. The pen and the ledger. Two instruments of power. Sepia, controlled tension.

slides.text: And then, in December 1920, a small man in a loincloth boarded a train toward Chhattisgarh. He did not come as a conqueror. He did not come as a missionary. He came because a farmer named Babu Chhotelal Srivastava had refused to pay an unjust canal tax, and the resistance in Kandel village had become too large for the British to ignore — and too important for the Congress to abandon. Chhattisgarh had given India its first Hindi newspaper, its most fearless social reformers, a warrior tradition that stretched back three thousand years. Now it was about to give Gandhi his most unexpected lesson: that the soil of Dakshin Kosal did not need to be taught how to resist. It needed only to be witnessed. This is that story.
slides.visualDescription: A lone train moving through a dark Chhattisgarh night — headlamp cutting through dense forest. Inside, Gandhi's face in the window reflection, eyes calm, resolute. Outside, a vast, ancient, watchful land receives him. The forests, the forts, the rivers — all lit by a waning moon. The sense of two histories about to collide. Gold light. Ink-wash, cinematic.

slides.text: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was an eminent independence activist and an influential political leader who played a major role in India's struggle for independence. Gandhi is known by different names — Mahatma, a great soul; Bapu, father in Gujarati; and Father of the Nation.
slides.visualDescription: Portrait of Gandhi — round glasses, gentle eyes, iconic profile. Dramatic rim lighting against dark background. The names Mahatma, Bapu, Father of the Nation orbit his silhouette in different scripts. Reverential, timeless.

slides.text: Gandhi began his activism as an Indian immigrant in South Africa in the early 1900s and became a leading figure in India's struggle for independence from Great Britain in the years following World War I. He often wore only a loincloth and shawl.
slides.visualDescription: Young Gandhi in South Africa — suited, determined, walking alone on a road. Then Gandhi in loincloth and shawl walking barefoot through Indian village. Two images of the same man, the transformation of a lifetime. Ink illustration.

slides.text: In South Africa, Gandhi felt racial discrimination towards blacks and Indians. He faced humiliation on several occasions, due to which he decided to fight racial discrimination. At that time, Indians and blacks in South Africa did not have the right to vote or even walk on the footpath.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi being thrown off a train in South Africa. Dramatic angle from the platform — the train door, a suited figure falling, British officers watching. Stark black and white with a slash of red. Sense of injustice and awakening.

slides.text: Gandhi strongly opposed this and eventually succeeded in establishing an organization called Indian National Congress in the year 1894. He returned to India in the year 1915 after living in South Africa for 21 years.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi standing at a podium with Indian National Congress banner in South Africa, a crowd of Indians and Black Africans before him. Ship on the ocean at sunrise — Gandhi at the bow looking toward the horizon. Homecoming. Hope.

slides.text: Gopal Krishna Gokhale, a senior leader of the Indian National Congress, invited Gandhi to join India's struggle for independence against British rule. In the year 1915, Gandhi came to India and toured the villages of the country to prepare the strategy for the freedom struggle.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi meeting Gopal Krishna Gokhale — two men shaking hands, mutual respect between them. Then Gandhi walking barefoot through Indian villages, children following. Dusty roads. A man learning his country from the ground up.

slides.text: Gandhi gave the name of Satyagraha to his entire non-violent method of work. Satyagraha for him meant the exercise of pure self-force against all kinds of injustice, tyranny, and exploitation. Gandhi said that Satyagraha can be adopted by anyone.
slides.visualDescription: A massive banyan tree with roots reaching in all directions — visual metaphor for Satyagraha. Gandhi's spinning charkha in close-up, thread being drawn. Split panel: armed soldiers on left, unarmed people standing firm on right. Philosophy made visible.

slides.text: In his thoughts, Satyagraha was like a banyan tree that has innumerable branches. Champaran and Bardoli Satyagrahas were done by Gandhi not only to get material benefits for the people but to oppose the unjust attitude of the then British rule.
slides.visualDescription: Indigo farmers of Champaran standing in their fields, Gandhi among them. Farmers of Bardoli on another panel. Two struggles, one method. Ink illustration, sepia and blue-green palette, the ground itself as a battlefield of ideas.

slides.text: The great scientist Albert Einstein said of Gandhi that future generations will find it difficult to believe that such a man — made of flesh and blood — ever came to earth. Gandhi's ideology not only inspired people all over the world but also played an important role in transforming India.
slides.visualDescription: Einstein at his desk, looking up with wonder. The quote floating beside him as golden text. World map with connecting lines from India to South Africa, USA, Myanmar — showing Gandhi's global reach. Awe, scale, legacy.

slides.text: Mahatma Gandhi inspired the world's great moral and political leaders such as Martin Luther King Jr., Nelson Mandela, and the Dalai Lama, and influenced social and political movements in Latin America, Asia, the Middle East, and Europe.
slides.visualDescription: Portraits of Martin Luther King Jr., Nelson Mandela, Aung San Suu Kyi arranged around Gandhi's central silhouette. Lines of influence connecting them. Globe in background. The reach of one man's idea across oceans and decades.

slides.text: Mahatma Gandhi is an indelible name, despite only two visits to Chhattisgarh. Chhattisgarh played an important role under the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi in the campaigns being run against the slavery of the British in India.
slides.visualDescription: Map of India zooming into Chhattisgarh. The region glows as if awakening — warm amber light spreading from it. Congress flag being raised in a village square. Pride, identity, belonging. Colonial-era ink-wash style.

slides.text: Gandhi infused a political, social, and economic consciousness within the entire state; the region of Chhattisgarh was not untouched by his efforts. In 1915, Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi returned to India from South Africa with a successful experiment of Satyagraha.
slides.visualDescription: A single flame spreading from one lamp to hundreds across a dark landscape — visual metaphor for Gandhi's ideological influence spreading through Chhattisgarh. Ink illustration, warm gold against deep black.

slides.text: When he returned after traveling all over the country on the advice of Gopal Krishna Gokhale, he understood the plight of the people of the country and the ill effects of British slavery. Chhattisgarh was a part of the Central Provinces.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi traveling by third-class rail across India — looking out a train window at passing villages, fields, and forests. The landscape shifts from city to jungle to paddy field. A man learning a country's wounds. Sepia, motion.

slides.text: After the death of Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak in 1920, Mahatma Gandhi emerged as the biggest leader of the Congress party, whose influence was also seen in Chhattisgarh. When the non-cooperation movement started in India, farmers in the Dhamtari region protested against the tax imposed on the canal water.
slides.visualDescription: Portrait of Lokmanya Tilak, somber, funeral pyre fading behind him. Then Gandhi stepping forward into the light — the passing of leadership. Farmers of Dhamtari standing in flooded paddy fields, British tax notice in hand. Transition of eras.

slides.text: Babu Chhotelal Srivastava had started the Kandel Satyagraha, which at the Congress party level, leaders like Pandit Sundarlal Sharma contributed to its widening. At the same time, in December 1920, the Congress session was to be held in Nagpur.
slides.visualDescription: Babu Chhotelal Srivastava standing firm before a group of farmers in Kandel village, fist raised. Behind him, flooded canal water and paddy fields. A leader emerging from ordinary soil. Ink illustration, determined expression.

slides.text: Sensing the situation, Pt. Sundarlal Sharma went to Calcutta because Gandhi was about to come from Calcutta to Nagpur. Pt. Sharma informed Gandhi about the Kandel Satyagraha and accompanied him to Raipur.
slides.visualDescription: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma boarding a train, determination on his face, destination Calcutta written on a board. Then: two figures in a train compartment at night — Sharma and Gandhi in intimate conversation by lamplight. The mission.

slides.text: By this time Gandhi's personality had already had an impact on the British. In 1917, indigo farmers had agitated in Champaran; a leader named Rajkumar Shukla had brought Mahatma Gandhi from Calcutta to Champaran.
slides.visualDescription: Split scene: Champaran indigo fields on left, Kandel canal and paddy on right. Same pattern of farmer resistance, same British injustice, different land. British official reading a telegram, face turning pale: Gandhi is coming.

slides.text: When the British came to know that Gandhi was coming to support the farmers of Champaran, they immediately formed a committee to resolve it, and the same happened in the case of Kandel Satyagraha in Chhattisgarh. The British accepted the demands of Kandel Satyagrahis even before Mahatma Gandhi reached Raipur.
slides.visualDescription: British officers hastily signing documents, withdrawing anti-farmer orders. Sweat on their brows. A telegraph machine clicking urgently. The power of Gandhi's name alone — a weapon without violence. Tension releasing into relief.

slides.text: Thus Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi had his first stay in Chhattisgarh. On December 20, 1920, Pt. Ravi Shankar Shukla, Thakur Pyarelal Singh, Sakharam Dubey, and others welcomed him on the platform at Raipur.
slides.visualDescription: Raipur railway platform, December 1920. A crowd waiting. Leaders in the front. The train arrives slowly. Ground-level shot — the crowd's feet, then hands reaching forward, then sandals stepping onto the platform. Gandhi arrives.

slides.text: Gandhi was lodged in Barrister Thakkar's bungalow in Raipur. Gandhi was accompanied by prominent leaders of the Khilafat Movement — Shaukat Ali and his brother Muhammad Ali. In the evening, Mahatma Gandhi addressed a huge general meeting.
slides.visualDescription: A grand colonial-era bungalow in Raipur — Gandhi welcomed at the entrance by Barrister Thakkar. Shaukat Ali and Muhammad Ali with him, all in white. The evening meeting ground filling with people as lamps are lit. Fifteen thousand faces.

slides.text: That place is famous today as Gandhi Chowk in Raipur. Speeches of Gandhi and Maulana Shaukat Ali were held in the massive presence of a crowd of about 15 thousand people. Gandhi gave the message of patriotism and was active in national programs.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi at the podium, Gandhi Chowk, Raipur 1920. A sea of fifteen thousand faces lit by lamps and torches. Shaukat Ali standing nearby, broad-shouldered. The energy of a nation awakening. Night sky above, stars and flags.

slides.text: Shaukat Ali jocularly said: 'I am like an elephant and Gandhi is like a goat.' People laughed. Then Maulana Shaukat Ali further said: 'Even if I die, it will not be of any use, but Gandhi is still useful for everyone, and will remain useful even after death.'
slides.visualDescription: Maulana Shaukat Ali — large, commanding — speaking at the podium. Gandhi seated beside him, small and still. The crowd laughing, then growing thoughtful. A moment of wit that reveals profound truth. Warm lamplight, night setting.

slides.text: Gandhi was collecting funds for the Tilak Swaraj Fund during his stay in Raipur and Dhamtari. They received cash, gold, and silver jewelry as donations. The women openly donated to the Tilak Fund; a large number of Muslim women attended the meeting.
slides.visualDescription: Women of all communities — Hindu and Muslim — at a gathering in Machilabad, Tatyapara, Raipur. Gold rings and jewelry placed in Gandhi's bag. Hands reaching forward with offerings. Unity, sacrifice, purpose. Lamplight and saris.

slides.text: The way the people experienced Gandhi's personality is captured in the words of freedom fighter Prabhu Lal Kabra: 'I saw Gandhi on the platform of Raipur — someone told that he was sitting in the third-class compartment, the public ran on the same side.'
slides.visualDescription: The Raipur platform: leaders descending from first and second class compartments. The crowd ignoring them, running toward the third-class end. Then: Gandhi at the door of the third-class compartment, wearing Lungi and Bandage Kurta, hands folded.

slides.text: 'People saw that Gandhi, wearing a Lungi and Bandage Kurta, was standing at the door of the third-class compartment with folded hands, till then the train started moving. Seeing Gandhi going in the third class, the public got emotional after realising his simplicity.'
slides.visualDescription: Close-up of Gandhi's face at the train door — eyes gentle, hands folded in namaste, the train slowly moving. Around him, a blur of reaching hands and emotional faces. The simplicity of the man against the enormity of the moment. Sepia.

slides.text: 'People became convinced that only Gandhi can lead the poor and downtrodden Indian people properly.' The Raipur District Congress Committee was formed on this same day. Pt. Ravi Shankar Shukla was made its first secretary.
slides.visualDescription: Ravi Shankar Shukla signing the founding papers of the Raipur District Congress Committee by lamplight. Around him, other leaders witness. The formation of a permanent structure of resistance. Ink on paper. History being made.

slides.text: Following the Amritsar Congress of 1919, at which the Khilafat Movement was endorsed and Non-Cooperation was adopted as a political weapon, the District Conference was held at Raipur in the year 1920. A public meeting was held on 17 March 1920 and a Khilafat sub-committee was formed.
slides.visualDescription: District Conference hall in Raipur, 1920. Leaders of all communities seated together. A Khilafat sub-committee being formed — Muslim and Hindu leaders standing side by side. Ravi Shankar Shukla's words: We are no more Hindu and Muslims, but Hindustanis.

slides.text: When Asgar Ali thanked the Hindu brethren for their sympathy for the Muslim cause, Ravi Shankar Shukla retorted: 'We are no more Hindu and Muslims, but Hindustanis in the strictest sense.' Such was the spirit of those times.
slides.visualDescription: Ravi Shankar Shukla standing, pointing outward, making his declaration. Asgar Ali beside him, moved. The crowd listening in a moment of unity. The words floating as illuminated text: We are Hindustanis in the strictest sense. Powerful.

slides.text: Gandhi visited Dhamtari and Kurud also, where people expressed their regard by a good deal of contribution to the Fund. It was in such an atmosphere that the Raipur District Committee was formed. Those were the days of brisk and militant political activities.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi in a motor car on the road to Dhamtari — crowds lining the route, throwing flowers. Kurud village in the distance. The landscape of Chhattisgarh at its most alive — roads of revolution, fields of hope. December 1920.

slides.text: Gandhi came to Chhattisgarh twice — the first time as Mohandas, the second time as a Mahatma. During both these visits Gandhi influenced the society and every person of Chhattisgarh. Thousands of leaders were influenced by Gandhi's personality and engaged in the service of the country for life.
slides.visualDescription: Two silhouettes of Gandhi — young Mohandas of 1920 and the elder Mahatma of 1933 — walking toward each other on a Chhattisgarh road, merging into one. Grid of portraits of all the leaders he inspired surrounding them. Gold light.

slides.text: The soil of Dakshin Kosal — present-day Chhattisgarh — lit up with the blood of its first martyr son, and this light further set fire to the piles of dry leaves of the rebellions. Next: Episode 2 — Blood of the First Martyr.
slides.visualDescription: A candle flame in darkness, reflecting on the ancient soil of Chhattisgarh. The flame grows, illuminating the faces of tribal warriors, freedom fighters, ordinary farmers. Title card fades in: Episode 2 — Blood of the First Martyr.
